Air nanobubble simultaneously enhances hydrolysis and methane yield of 
sludge temperature phased-anaerobic digestion☆
Ziying Xu a, Tianfeng Wang a,*
, Cheng Peng a, Yutong Feng a, Xin Fan a, Xuan Yang a,  
Wenqi Gao b, Qingfang Zhang a
a College of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China
b School of Civil Engineering, Lanzhou Institute of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• NBW increased TAN by 7.8%-13.7% in 
the hydrolysis phase.
• NBW increased ultimate methane yield 
by 23.3%-41.5%.
• NBW improved the diversity and rich­
ness of microorganisms in hydrolysis.
• Thermophilic conditions facilitate low 
VS/TS sludge anaerobic digestion.
• The combination of NBW and MEC 
achieved efficient anaerobic digestion.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Ammonia
Sludge particle size
Fluorescence intensity
Bacteria
Archaea
A B S T R A C T
Nanobubble water (NBW) or temperature-phased anaerobic digestion assisted by microbial electrolysis cell 
(MEC-TPAD) can promote sludge hydrolysis and methanogenesis. However, the role of the combined application 
of NBW and MEC-TPAD in terms of anaerobic performance and related microbial properties remains unclear. 
This study investigated the impact of Air-NBW on hydrolysis and methanogenesis of dewatered sludge MEC- 
TPAD. Under different temperatures, NBW increased ammonia nitrogen by 7.8%-13.7% in the hydrolysis 
phase and ultimate methane yield by 23.3%-41.5%. NBW can significantly promote hydrolysis under mesophilic- 
mesophilic conditions, while it can promote substantially methanogenesis under thermophilic-thermophilic 
conditions. Moreover, NBW increased the diversity and richness of microorganisms in hydrolysis. As to bacte­
ria, NBW increased the relative abundance (RA) of Firmicutes but decreased the RA of Proteobacteria. As to 
archaea, NBW increased the RA of Methanosarcina in hydrolysis but decreased it in methanogenesis. NBW 
synchronized with MEC-TPAD improved hydrolysis and methanogenesis of the dewatered sludge digestion 
process.
☆This article is part of a special issue entitled: ‘ABTCNN 2024’ published in Bioresource Technology.

1. Introduction
Dewatered sludge (DWS) has become a critical issue in municipal 
wastewater treatment plants because the presence of harmful sub­
stances, heavy metals, and pathogenic microorganisms in DWS increases 
the potential risks to humans and the environment (Li et al., 2018). 
Temperature-phased anaerobic digestion (TPAD) has been extensively 
employed for the treatment of dewatered sludge (Wang et al., 2018). 
Thermophilic conditions effectively destroy pathogens and significantly 
enhance volatile solids (VS) removal in the hydrolysis phase, whereas 
mesophilic conditions mitigate volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation in 
the methanogenesis phase (Sillero et al., 2023). However, the excessive 
ammonia produced during thermophilic hydrolysis in TPAD may inhibit 
the activity of methanogenesis microorganisms (Sillero et al., 2023).
Coupling microbial electrolysis cell (MEC) with TPAD has been 
recognized as a promising technique to alleviate the inhibition of 
methanogen activity (Yuan et al., 2022). MEC modified the microbial 
community by enriching electroactive microorganisms and metha­
nogens, which led to increased methane yield (Kanellos et al., 2024). 
MEC can also overcome thermodynamic limitations to accelerate the 
degradation of organic matter by applying voltage (Wang et al., 2022a). 
The intermittent MEC-TPAD increased ultimate methane yield (UMY) in 
the DWS by 118.9 % compared with the control group (Peng et al., 
2024). However, the research of Peng et al. (2024) had a low total solids 
(TS) with 12.8 % and a high VS/TS with 63.0 % of DWS, which was 
conducive to the degradation of organic matter. Furthermore, distilled 
water was added prior to the digestion process to reduce the TS to 8.2 %, 
which improved mass transfer efficiency.
In actual circumstances, the TS of DWS is generally as high as about 
20 % (Wang et al., 2024a). Excessively high TS will reduce the fluidity of 
digestate and affect the transfer efficiency of nutrients to microorgan­
isms (Abid et al., 2021). Moreover, due to improper sewage treatment 
and low sediment interception rate, DWS often exhibits low organic 
matter content (VS/TS < 50 %) (Shi et al., 2023). These factors are 
detrimental to the hydrolysis of sludge. In the case of high TS and low 
VS/TS, the hydrolysis of MEC-TPAD may still be insufficient (Shi et al., 
2023; Wang et al., 2022a). Therefore, it is necessary to add a reasonable 
medium on the basis of MEC-TPAD to reduce the solid content and 
improve the hydrolysis performance.
Nanobubble water (NBW) is a water body containing nanobubbles 
with a diameter < 1 μm and has the advantages of high stability, gas 
solubility, and negative zeta potential compared with deionized water 
(Pei et al., 2024). The high mobility of NBW facilitates the reduction of 
sludge viscosity and enhances nutrient transfer to microorganisms 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). Furthermore, NBW enhanced the degradation 
of the complex substrate by releasing reactive oxygen species while 
stimulating enzyme activity to improve microbial community structure 
(Fan et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2024). Additionally, O2-NBW and Air-NBW 
enable the creation of micro-oxygen conditions for facultative micro­
organisms to promote substrate hydrolysis, thereby improving hydro­
lysis performance (Pei et al., 2024). NBW can stimulate the activity of 
methanogens, thereby increasing methane yield (Hou et al., 2024). Air- 
NBW increased methane yield from sludge by 23.0 % (Hou et al., 2021). 
Adding CO2, Air, He, and N2 to NBW improved the methane yield of 
DWS by 32.0 %, 27.9 %, 16.0 %, and 9.2 %, respectively (Wang et al., 
2024a). The potential synergistic effects of NBW and MEC-TPAD on 
hydrolysis and methanogenesis warrant further investigation. Currently, 
there is limited research on the combined application of NBW and MEC, 
and the effects of NBW on the digestion performance and microbial 
community structure of MEC-TPAD remain largely unknown.
In this study, a low-cost and readily available Air-NBW coupled with 
intermittent MEC-TPAD was selected to (1) explore the effects of the 
new AD system on the hydrolysis efficiency, substrate degradation and 
methane yield of DWS; (2) 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed the 
alteration of bacterial and archaeal communities by Air-NBW under 
different temperature conditions to better understand the metabolic 
mechanism of microorganisms in AD. This research contributes to 
developing a novel strategy for the combined application of NBW and 
MEC as an anaerobic treatment of DWS to increase renewable energy 
production.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Thickened sludge and DWS were acquired from a wastewater treat­
ment plant in Lanzhou utilizing an oxidation ditch process. Seed sludge 
was obtained by incubating thickened sludge under thermophilic and 
mesophilic conditions. The properties of DWS and different seed sludge 
were determined (see Supplementary Material). DWS (VS/TS < 50.0 
%) was the low organic matter content sludge (Shi et al., 2023). The 
design of the intermittent MEC anaerobic digesters was described by 
Peng et al. (2024). Air-NBW was prepared as described in Wang et al. 
(2024a).
2.2. Experimental process
At the beginning of the experiment, thermophilic or mesophilic seed 
sludge was added as an inoculum to DWS with Air-NBW or deionized 
water. The mass ratio of seed sludge, DWS, and Air-NBW or deionized 
water = 1: 5: 5, totaling 880 g, was added to each digester. Nitrogen was 
utilized to purge for 2–4 min to ensure an anaerobic environment in the 
digesters.
To determine the optimal temperatures for the hydrolysis and 
methanogenic phases in AD, respectively, the digesters were divided 
into three temperature conditions: T-T (sustained thermophilic condi­
tions), M−M (sustained mesophilic conditions) and T-M (thermophilic 
+ mesophilic conditions). Previous studies have found that the residence 
time of the hydrolysis phase was generally 2 ± 1 days (Ge et al., 2010; 
Mehari and Chang, 2022), so the T-M digesters chose to change the 
temperature after 2 days. The hydrolysis phase was set to be 0–2 days 
and the methanogenesis phase to be 3–41 days. After 2 days of the 
experiment, thermophilic seed sludge (80 g) was added to T-T digesters 
and mesophilic seed sludge (80 g) to T-M and M−M digesters. 
Depending on the addition of NBW or deionized water, the three tem­
perature conditions were labeled TTN, TTD, TMN, TMD, MMN, and 
MMD. Digesters from different groups were placed in the corresponding 
water baths at different times (thermophilic for 55 ± 1 ◦C and meso­
philic for 35 ± 1 ◦C). All groups were treated with MEC, and three 
parallel experiments were performed in each group.
2.3. Methods of analysis
TS, VS, pH, total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), and soluble chemical 
oxygen demand (SCOD) were measured in the same way as in APHA 
(1998). Free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was analyzed utilizing standard 
formulas related to temperature, TAN, and pH (Hansen et al., 1998). A 
nanoparticle size analyzer was used to analyze sludge particle size 
(Malvern, Nano ZS90, UK). Methane content and VFA were assessed 
utilizing a gas chromatograph (Rui Hong, SP-7890Plus, China) equipped 
with a flame ionization detector and an organic acid analysis column 
(30 m × 320 μm × 0.5 μm). The set parameters of the column and de­
tector were consistent with those used by Peng et al. (2024). A wet-type 
gas flow meter was used to analyze the biogas volume (Alpha, LML-2, 
China). A Spectro fluorophotometer was utilized to gain three- 
dimensional fluorescence excitation and emission matrix (3D-EEM) 
scans (Hitachi, F4600, Japan).
DNA was taken from sludge samples and then subjected to Illumina 
sequencing. Specific primer sequences 341F (CCTACGGGNGGCWG­
CAG) and 806R (GGACTACHVGGGTATCTAAT) were utilized to amplify 
the V3-V4 regions of bacteria. Specific primer sequences Arch519F 
(CAGCMGCCGCGGTAA) and Arch915R (GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT)

were utilized to amplify the V4-V5 regions of archaea. The sequenced 
microbial data have been included online (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih. 
gov). PRJNA1151961 and PRJNA1151965 were the accession number.
2.4. Statistical analysis
Results Data were presented as the mean ± standard deviation of 
data from three parallel trials, and one-way analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) was performed using SPSS version 27.0. Statistical signifi­
cance was set at p < 0.05. The Duncan’s test and principal component 
analysis (PCA) were also performed using SPSS. The modified Gompertz 
formula was utilized to fit the methane yield (Zhang et al., 2021). The 
humification index (HIX) was calculated using the emission intensity 
region at 254 nm Ex (linear interpolation) (Guan et al., 2024). 
Figures were drawn using Origin 2018 (OriginLab, Massachusetts, USA).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. pH, TAN, sludge particle size, and VFA
The pH of all groups ranged from 7.0 to 8.5 (Fig. 1a), which was in 
line with the acceptable range for anaerobic microbial growth and 
metabolism in AD (Zhang et al., 2021). TAN can reflect the AD system’s 
hydrolysis effects in the sludge (Wang et al., 2023). Methanogen activity 
may be inhibited when TAN exceeds 1500 mg L-1 (Wang et al., 2024a). 
On day 2, the TAN of the hydrolysis phase in T-M groups was increased 
by 227.1 %-239.6 % (p < 0.001) compared with that in M−M groups 
(Fig. 1d). In the hydrolysis phase, TAN in the NBW-added groups was 
improved by 7.8 %-13.7 % compared with the control groups. Among 
them, TAN was significantly increased in the T-T and M−M groups (p < 
0.05), with the highest rate of increase observed in the M−M groups. 
NBW could promote the hydrolysis ability of the AD system, with the 
most pronounced effects observed under mesophilic conditions. On day 
41, the TAN of the groups was T-T > T-M > M−M in descending order. 
Duncan’s test based on day 41 sample data showed no correlation be­
tween the TAN of the three types of temperature conditions, which were 
significantly different (Fig. 1b). However, NBW did not produce a sig­
nificant difference in TAN between groups except for the M−M groups.
The hydrolysis performance of AD under thermophilic conditions is 
superior to that under mesophilic conditions (Liu et al., 2013). Elevated 
temperatures are conducive to the improvement of hydrolysis perfor­
mance. However, they also impact microbial diversity. Compared with 
thermophilic conditions, the types of hydrolytic bacteria under meso­
philic conditions are more abundant (Chen et al., 2021a), and NBW 
could promote the activity of more types of hydrolytic bacteria to 
improve the hydrolysis performance. Consequently, NBW increased 
TAN more aggressively under mesophilic conditions. Moreover, tem­
perature conditions significantly influenced TAN more than NBW. 
Different NBW increased TAN during AD by 6.4 %-10.1 % (Hou et al., 
2022; Wang et al., 2024a). Compared with mesophilic conditions, 
thermophilic conditions during AD increased TAN by 59.0 %-173.7 % 
(Peng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). These results suggested that 
temperature conditions are a more critical factor influencing AD.
FAN can penetrate the cell membrane of methanogens, making 
methanogens toxic (Zhang et al., 2021). The FAN in the T-T groups was 
significantly higher than in the T-M and M−M groups (see Supple­
mentary Material). The activity of acetate-nutrient methanogens may 
be inhibited when FAN exceeds 588 mg L-1 (Moerland et al., 2021). 
From day 6 to day 41, the acetate-nutrient methanogens in the T-T di­
gesters may be inhibited. However, hydrogenotrophic methanogens 
were more tolerant to high ammonia environments, and the activity of 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens could not recover from ammonia stress 
when FAN exceeds 900 mg L-1 (Wang et al., 2022b).
The smaller sludge particle size means the AD process was carried 
out more thoroughly (Guo et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2022). Under 
thermophilic conditions, the sludge particle size of the NBW-added 
group was smaller than that of the control (Fig. 1c). Conversely, under 
mesophilic conditions, the sludge particle size of the groups with NBW

was larger than that of the control groups. This discrepancy may be 
attributed to the limited promotional effects of NBW, where the nano­
bubbles generate •OH radicals upon collapse (Chuenchart et al., 2021; 
Zhu et al., 2024). It can promote effective sludge solubilization and 
further degradation of cellular materials in small sludge particles (Yang 
et al., 2019) while having almost no effects on larger sludge particles. 
The hydrolysis performance under thermophilic conditions is superior to 
that under mesophilic conditions (Liu et al., 2013), resulting in a greater 
number of small particles in thermophilic environments compared with 
mesophilic ones. A specific quantity of NBW can consume a certain 
number of small particles, leading to a higher residual count of small 
particles under thermophilic conditions than under mesophilic condi­
tions. Temperature conditions made a large difference in sludge particle 
size compared with NBW, thereby representing a more critical factor in 
influencing sludge particle size.
VFA is the product of hydrolysis in AD, SCOD represents the content 
of soluble reductive matter, and the trends of SCOD and VFA are similar 
(Shi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). The SCOD and VFA were higher in 
the T-M groups than in the T-T groups on day 6 (Fig. 2 and Supple­
mentary Material). This observation may be attributed to the addition 
of mesophilic seed sludge and changing the temperature conditions from 
thermophilic to mesophilic, the microorganisms in the T-M groups had 
not fully adapted to the new ambient temperature, and the ability to 
degrade organic matter had not yet been restored (Postawa et al., 2020). 
The SCOD of the T-T groups was at a high level, while the VFA was 
shallow at the late stage of AD. The thermophilic conditions that pro­
moted the degradation of VFA and led to the accumulation of some re­
fractory organics (heterocyclic-N compounds, e.g., pyrimidine, pyrrole, 
and pyridine) to increase the SCOD (Zhang et al., 2024).
3.2. Three-dimensional fluorescence excitation and emission matrix 
spectra
In the 3D-EEM spectra, regions I and II are simple aromatic proteins; 
region III is fulvic acids; region IV is soluble microbial by-products; and 
region V is humic acids (Guan et al., 2024). The fluorescence intensity 
was maximized in region V, while it was nearly zero in the other regions 
(Fig. 3). In terms of temperature conditions, the fluorescence intensity of 
region V was M−M (148.3–149.1) > T-M (62.4–66.7) > T-T (9.0–11.7) 
on day 41. Humic acids decreased with increasing thermophilic time 
(Warwick et al., 1997). In addition, adding NBW reduced the fluores­
cence intensity. Humic acids were an intermediate product of the 
bioconversion of organic matter to methane during AD and had a 
complex redox function (Wang et al., 2021). The nanobubbles released 
chemical energy upon collapse and were accompanied by the produc­
tion of •OH radicals, which had strong oxidizing properties helping to 
degrade complex humic acids (Hou et al., 2024). The addition of 25.0 % 
nanobubbles slightly reduced the fluorescence intensity in region V of 
aerobic-activated sludge, and NBW accelerated the degradation of 
humic acids (Xiao et al., 2021). The fluorescence intensities of TTN, 
TMN, and MMN groups were reduced by 23.1 %, 6.4 %, and 0.5 %, 
respectively, compared with the control groups without NBW. This 
might be because the T-T groups contain fewer humic acids, resulting in 
a greater amplitude of change in fluorescence intensity. HIX indicates 
the degree of humification of dissolved organic matter (Guan et al., 
2024). The trend observed in HIX was consistent with the fluorescence 
intensity in region V, thereby demonstrating that both NBW and ther­
mophilic conditions facilitated the degradation of humic acids. The in­
crease in humic acids inhibited the ability to produce methane (Li et al., 
2023). Consequently, the fluorescence intensity of humic acids exhibited 
a negative correlation with methane yield, consistent with the results of 
methane yield (Table 1).
3.3. Methane yield
The models were fitted with Gompertz (Table 1), and the fitted re­
sults were subjected to Duncan’s test. The results showed that the lag 
phase of the digesters was significantly different under different tem­
peratures (p < 0.05). The longest lag phase was observed in the T-M 
digesters, attributed to the microorganisms needing time to adapt to the 
new environmental conditions (Postawa et al., 2020). Under theoretical 
conditions, the Rm of the T-T digesters was the largest and significantly 
different from the other groups (p < 0.05). It has been found that under 
thermophilic conditions, the larger the Rm, the smaller the λ (Arelli 
et al., 2021), indicating that the T-T digesters can produce more 
methane while shortening the reaction period. The peak daily methane 
yield rate in TTN was higher and appeared earlier than in TTD (Table 1
and Fig. 4a). NBW accelerated the degradation of the substrate and the

reduction of λ (Hou et al., 2021).
On day 41, the T-M digesters enhanced the UMY by 15.0 %-25.8 % (p 
< 0.05) compared with the M−M digesters (Table 1 and Fig. 4c). 
Thermophilic conditions are more effective in promoting the hydrolysis 
of the complex substrate (Wang et al., 2024b). The T-T digesters 
enhanced the UMY by 46.6 %-68.4 % (p < 0.001) compared with the T- 
M digesters, which suggested that the methanogenesis phase of the AD 
process in this study is more suitable for thermophilic conditions. 
However, mesophilic conditions can promote the activity of metha­
nogens during the methanogenesis phase to ensure the stability of 
methane yield (Chen et al., 2021b). The reason for this difference could 
be the low VS/TS of DWS (26.4 %) (Table 1), which was lower than that 
(74.0 %) of Chen et al. (2021b). Temperature can affect the fluidity and 
mass transfer efficiency of digestate, and substrate with low organic 
matter content cannot be degraded as expected under mesophilic con­
ditions (Rodríguez-Jim´enez et al., 2022). Thermophilic conditions can 
improve the efficiency of energy transfer and accelerate the consump­
tion of soluble nutrients, leading to more complete hydrolysis and 
organic matter utilization than mesophilic conditions without worrying 
about VFA accumulation (Fig. 2), thereby improving methane yield 
(Jomnonkhaow et al., 2024). Compared with mesophilic conditions, 
there was a 21.9 %-35.8 % increase in methane yield when the VS/TS of 
the substrate was 34.2 % under thermophilic conditions (Zhang et al., 
2021).
The UMY of the NBW-added groups was significantly enhanced by 
23.3 %-41.5 % (p < 0.05) compared with the control groups, respec­
tively (Fig. 4c). This finding aligns with the results of Wang et al. 
(2024a), which reported that Air-NBW improved the methane yield of 
DWS by 27.9 %. NBW can significantly improve methane yield by pro­
moting enzyme activity (hydrolase and coenzyme F420) and increasing 
electron transfer (Chuenchart et al., 2021). Among them, NBW pro­
moted the most methane yield in the T-T groups, with 41.5 % (p < 
0001). Under thermophilic conditions, the mass transfer efficiency of 
digestate was higher (Rodríguez-Jim´enez et al., 2022). The sludge par­
ticle size was the smallest in the T-T groups, and a large number of 
charged ions on the surface of the nanobubbles would release chemical 
energy to produce •OH radicals, which promoted the further degrada­
tion of organic matter in small particle sludge by microorganisms (Yang 
et al., 2019). TTN increased UMY by 161.0 % (p < 0.001) compared 
with MMD. The coupling of thermophilic-thermophilic TPAD with NBW 
represented one of the optimal strategies to improve the methane yield 
of DWS with low VS/TS.

3.4. Bacterial community
The Chao is proportional to species richness, and the Shannon is 
proportional to species diversity (¨Oztep et al., 2023). NBW promoted the 
diversity and richness of the bacterial community during the hydrolysis 
phase (Fig. 5a). This finding aligns with the results reported by Wang 
et al. (2020), which indicate that the microaerobic environment created 
by Air-NBW facilitated direct interspecific electron transfer (DIET) and 
improved the diversity and richness of microorganisms during the hy­
drolysis phase.
Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, and Bacter­
oidota, were the top five dominant bacteria during AD (Fig. 5b). 
Compared with mesophilic conditions, the relative abundance (RA) of 
Firmicutes (6.5 %-46.0 %) and Actinobacteriota (0.9 %-4.0 %) increased, 
and the RA of Proteobacteria (1.8 %-14.8 %), Chloroflexi (1.4 %-6.4 %) 
and Bacteroidota (3.9 %-16.7 %) decreased under thermophilic condi­
tions (see Supplementary Material). Furthermore, the RA of Firmicutes 
(0.0 %-8.7 %) increased, and the RA of Proteobacteria (0.1 %-13.1 %) 
decreased because of the addition of NBW. PCA showed significant 
differences between the groups under different temperature conditions 
(see Supplementary Material). There were no significant differences 
between the NBW-added groups and the control groups. This implied the 
changes in the bacterial community were mainly controlled by 
temperature.
Both Firmicutes and Actinobacteriota were significantly and positively 
correlated (p < 0.01) with SCOD, TAN, UMY, and VFA (Fig. 5c). Fir­
micutes can break down complex carbohydrates and proteins to produce 
VFA, which is converted to H2 for utilization by hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens (Ali et al., 2024; ¨Oztep et al., 2023). Firmicutes were able to 
survive both thermophilic and mesophilic conditions. However, the 
promotion of hydrolysis increased SCOD and VFA under thermophilic 
conditions, which elevated the RA of Firmicutes. Furthermore, NBW 
increased the activity of hydrolytic enzymes, which further increased 
the RA of Firmicutes (Fan et al., 2021). Similarly, thermophilic condi­
tions elevated the RA of Actinobacteriota, and a large amount of organic 
matter was degraded and converted to acetate and H2 (de Sousa e Silva 
et al., 2024). Proteobacteria significantly and negatively correlated (p < 
0.01) with SCOD and VFA. It has been shown that the RA of Proteo­
bacteria decreased with increasing hydrolysis under thermophilic con­
ditions (Peng et al., 2024). Thus, Firmicutes dominated under 
thermophilic conditions, whereas Proteobacteria dominated under mes­
ophilic conditions. In addition, enhanced hydrolysis by adding NBW 
further decreased the RA of Proteobacteria (Fan et al., 2021).
3.5. Archaeal community
The number of bacteria was much greater than that of archaea, 
indicating that bacteria dominated the degradation of organic matter 
while archaea played a supplementary role in degrading organic matter 
(Fan et al., 2022). NBW promoted the diversity and richness of the 
archaeal community during the hydrolysis phase (Fig. 6a).
Methanothermobacter, 
Methanosaeta, 
Methanosarcina, 
Meth­
anobacterium, and Methanospirillum were the top five dominant archaea 
during AD (Fig. 6b). Compared with mesophilic conditions, the RA of 
Methanothermobacter (0.1 %-31.6 %) and Methanosarcina (0.1 %-4.2 %) 
increased, and the RA of Methanosaeta (7.9 %-14.8 %), Meth­
anobacterium (4.2 %-8.6 %), and Methanospirillum (0.5 %-1.2 %) 
decreased during both the hydrolysis and methanogenesis phases under 
thermophilic conditions (see Supplementary Material). Furthermore, 
NBW increased the RA of Methanosarcina (0.2 %-4.4 %) and Meth­
anospirillum (0.0 %-0.6 %) during the hydrolysis phase, decreased the 
RA of Methanosarcina (1.8 %-3.5 %) and Methanospirillum (0.0 %-1.1 %) 
during the methanogenesis phase. PCA showed significant differences 
between the groups under different temperature conditions (see Sup­
plementary Material). There were no significant differences between 
the NBW-added groups and the control groups. This meant that, like the 
bacterial community, changes in the archaeal community were pri­
marily controlled by temperature.
The hydrogenotrophic methanogens Methanothermobacter were 
significantly and positively correlated (p < 0.01) with SCOD, TAN, 
UMY, and VFA (Fig. 6c). Elevated levels of ammonia or VFA can lead to 
the enrichment of Methanothermobacter (Hori et al., 2006; Yan et al., 
2020). During the hydrolysis phase, thermophilic conditions promoted 
the production of large amounts of VFA and increased the TAN. Sub­
sequently, during the methanogenesis phase, thermophilic conditions 
promoted the degradation of organic matter, resulting in a continued 
increase in TAN. Additionally, Methanothermobacter has been shown to 
enhance methane generation under ammonia inhibition (Yan et al., 
2020). Consequently, Methanothermobacter had an elevated RA.
Mixed trophic methanogens Methanosarcina were significantly and 
positively correlated (p < 0.01) with pH, TAN, FAN, and UMY. Meth­
anosarcina could be stabilized under conditions of high ammonia levels 
and high pH levels (Wang et al., 2024b). Thermophilic conditions pro­
moted hydrolysis, generating large amounts of ammonia nitrogen, 
leading to elevated RA of Methanosarcina. Furthermore, NBW increased 
the RA of Methanosarcina during the hydrolysis phase and decreased the 
RA of Methanosarcina during the methanogenesis phase. This was

attributed to the fact that Methanosarcina is a facultative bacteria, and 
the microaerobic environment created by NBW enhanced the activity of 
Methanosarcina and accelerated the hydrolysis (Chuenchart et al., 2021). 
However, in the methanogenesis phase, where the effects of NBW was 
weakened, the disappearance of the microaerobic environment reduced 
the activity of the facultative bacteria, causing a decrease in the RA of 
Methanosarcina.
In the T-T groups, the archaeal community was dominated by 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens. The H2 produced by Firmicutes and 
Actinobacteriota was utilized by Methanothermobacter to increase 
methane yield. Firmicutes controlled the limited rate step of the AD, and 
thermophilic conditions promoted the hydrolysis of Firmicutes. NBW 
further enhanced the activity of Firmicutes and alleviated acid inhibition 
and ammonia inhibition (Hou et al., 2024). In addition to the role of 
microorganisms, the •OH radicals generated at the gas–liquid interface 
during the collapse of nanobubbles, along with elevated temperatures, 
can disrupt the stable structure of the complex substrate (Hou et al., 
2021; Liu et al., 2013). Collectively, these factors contributed to the 
improvement of AD performance.
All index results showed that the combined application of NBW and 
MEC did not inhibit or affect each other. The negative surface charge of 
NBW can increase the amount of electrons available at the electrode 
(Hou et al., 2024). MEC enriched electroactive microorganisms and 
methanogens on the electrode surface (Wang et al., 2022a), and the 
addition of NBW stimulated both microbial activity and electron transfer 
on the electrode surface, thereby activating the DIET mechanism within

the AD system and accelerating the electron transfer between microor­
ganisms (Liu et al., 2024). However, the specific change mechanisms 
underlying the combined effects of NBW and MEC on enzyme activity 
and metabolic pathways remain unclear, necessitating further 
investigation.
The combined application of NBW with MEC represents a promising 
approach. However, due to the instability of sludge organic matter, the 
effects of different temperature conditions on sludge AD may fluctuate. 
In the future, the combination of the application of MEC and nanobubble 
technology could be explored to address additional challenges, such as 
improving dehydration performance and reducing heavy metal content.
4. Conclusions
NBW synchronized with MEC-TPAD improved hydrolysis and 
methanogenesis of the DWS digestion process. Among them, the 
combined application of NBW and thermophilic-thermophilic TPAD is 
beneficial for AD of sludge with lower organic matter content. NBW 
significantly promoted hydrolysis under mesophilic-mesophilic condi­
tions, with TAN increased by 13.7 %. NBW significantly promoted 
methanogenesis under thermophilic-thermophilic conditions, with UMY 
increased by 41.5 %. NBW increased the diversity and richness of mi­
croorganisms in the hydrolysis phase, and the enriched functional mi­
croorganisms played an important role in improving AD performance. 
This research presents a new technological insight to improve the AD 
performance of DWS.
